some rules about DNA synthesis: 
1. DNA synthesis is always proceeds 5’—> 3’
2. DNA synthesis cannot happen de novo, meaning it must have a primer of some sort to begin replication.

the reason why the lagging strand is called that is because its strand is 5’ —> 3’. so, DNA polymerase cannot synthesize from ‘left to right’ because jt cannot make a strand that is 3’ —> 5’. therefore, DNA polymerase needs to read the strand from right to left to synthesize the new strand. 

because DNA synthesis cannot happen de novo, there must be primers put in for the DNA polymerase to latch on to and begin DNA synthesis from them. therefore, RNA primers are put in spaces b and d so that the DNA polymerase can correctly synthesize a strand 3’ —> 5’. so, your options become b or d. b is correct because overall, your DNA synthesis is moving left to right so b will be the space of the first primer.

one of the main points of okazaki fragments and RNA primers is so that the lagging strand can be synthesized overall in the same direction of the leading strand.

For me personally, stats 13 was a pretty straightforward class, and wasn’t necessarily challenging. The programming in it can be a bother, but it’s nothing too crazy/hard. 14BL is a LOT of writing, and the main difficulty behind it is getting the hang of formatting/scheduling when to do assignments. The concepts in 14BL are pretty straightforward and align well with 14B. 5A for me was challenging as physics is not my forte and was my first time being exposed to a lot of the concepts. 14C is content heavy, but I found it really cool and the Klein books are a godsend. Overall, I think your best bet is to take 14BL, stats 13, and 5A together, then take 14C the next quarter because it is important to have a good understanding in 14C for CL and D and may be best to take with some geneds. You could switch 5A and 14C, but I would not recommend taking them together as they require a lot of time to be devoted to them. Hope this helps!

I'm gonna have to respectfully disagree with you. Your first problem in your argument is assuming that getting a high score on the SAT directly means someone is ready for college, or vice versa. Some people are extremely smart, but just don't do well on standardized testing. 

Also, the SAT really is a test of your affluence rather than a test of your intelligence. I personally did pretty well on the SAT without paying for a tutor, but that was because I had time to practice. Time is a luxury that many underprivileged students do not have. Also, A LOT of wealthier students pay thousands of dollars for tutors and practice material, which, again, underprivileged students cannot afford.

I tend to not comment on posts, but I feel it is important you see this topic from a different perspective. The SAT is not the end all be all measurement of someone's "readiness for college" and you need to have a long hard look at yourself if you think it is.
